descriptor: Big-four Australian bank · Sep FY · reported in AUD

charts.title: Net Interest Income, Cash Profit & Net Income

sections.title: Capital, Funding & Balance Sheet
sections.subtitle: Bank FCFE is capitalised cash profit less capital retained, not operating cash flow less CapEx

charts.title: Book Value per Share
charts.annotation: Owner FCF in the DCF is FCFE (cash earnings after regulatory capital retention), not OCF less CapEx -- a bank's balance sheet growth is the reinvestment, so a conventional FCF chart is not meaningful here.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

loansDeposits.title: Loans and deposits
loansDeposits.content:
Net loans & advances is the bank's lending book; customer deposits is customer-funded liabilities. The gap between them is funded by wholesale debt and equity.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the DCF treats WBC's net debt as zero -- deposits and wholesale funding are the business, not leverage on top of it -- so there is no cash-vs-debt chart here as there would be for an operating company.

What to watch:

  • Deposit growth funding loan growth (lowers wholesale funding cost)
  • Loan book growth versus system credit growth

cet1.title: CET1 ratio and credit impairment charge
cet1.content:
CET1 (Common Equity Tier 1) ratio is APRA's core regulatory capital measure, risk-weighted assets as the denominator; APRA's minimum for a major bank is 10.25%. The credit impairment charge is the P&L provision for expected loan losses.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the DCF's FCFE base deducts capital retained to hold CET1 roughly flat as the loan book grows -- a falling CET1 ratio means less cash is available to shareholders than cash profit implies.

What to watch:

  • CET1 drifting toward the regulatory minimum
  • Impairment charge spiking in a credit cycle downturn

bvps.title: Book value per share
bvps.content:
Book value per share is shareholders' equity divided by shares outstanding.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: tangible book value (equity less intangibles) has recently been falling faster than reported BVPS as ordinary dividends and buybacks run ahead of organic FCFE -- see the DCF's last_fcf note.

What to watch:

  • BVPS growth versus ROE less payout ratio (the sustainable growth check)
  • Divergence between statutory and tangible book value

costIncomeRoe.title: Cost to income ratio and ROE
costIncomeRoe.content:
Cost to income ratio is operating expenses divided by operating income (lower is better efficiency); ROE is cash profit divided by average shareholders' equity.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: WBC has targeted mid-40s% CTI and low-teens ROE against major-bank peers running tighter; both are levers management calls out every half.

What to watch:

  • CTI trending down (efficiency program progress) or up (cost blowout)
  • ROE versus WBC's own cost of equity

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Net interest income is interest earned on loans less interest paid on deposits/funding -- a bank's core revenue line. Cash profit strips notable items from statutory net income and is management's preferred earnings measure.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the DCF's FCFE base starts from cash profit ex-notable items, not statutory net income, because notable items (remediation, hedge accounting) are treated as non-recurring.

What to watch:

  • Net interest margin pressure showing up as NII growing slower than the loan book
  • Cash profit vs statutory net income gap (size and recurrence of notable items)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
